utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, was there a matter you wanted to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A couple of matters that I need to raise at least in private session, possibly in closed session. It shan't take very long. May we go into private session first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your name is Muhamed Mujezinovic, born in 1949, a doctor by profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A graduate from Sarajevo, you returned from -- you went to Vitez to work in Vitez as a doctor, specialising in internal medicine, in the mid-1980s, working in a medical centre in Vitez and in the general hospital in Travnik? You could say "Yes" when I come to the end of a passage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, except that my first job was in Doboj. I was a general practitioner in Doboj first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you also specialise in occupational medicine and occupational diseases, and were you active as a doctor in the sports clubs in Vitez, also working occasionally for the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I can move to the second topic, and no doubt those representing the defendants will tell me if and when they want me to stop asking leading questions. Until 1990, in Vitez, was there simply one political party, but in 1990 did several parties and, in particular, did nationalist parties emerge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 1990, there was one leading party in Vitez, the League of Communists. There was the socialist alliance of the working people and the youth organisation. But by and large, it was all under the umbrella of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then after 1990, did nationalist parties emerge, namely the Croatian Democratic Community, the Serbian Democratic Party and the SDA as the nationalist parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they emerged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the other parties you've listed in the past and can list again, if asked? I'm not going to ask you to list them. I'm just saying you can list them, if asked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can list them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first president of the HDZ in Vitez was whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Professor Anto Valenta, rather, an engineer of applied chemistry, Anto Valenta.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he an acquaintance or friend of yours or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we knew one another, but we were not friends. Nor were we enemies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as the SDA is concerned, its first president was who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hajrudin Karic, an electrical engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the second president was whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Munib Kajmovic, a history professor in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He took the office of president roughly when, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The latter half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you involved in the party as a member from an early stage or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I became a member of the SDA sometime in September 1990, and I began to actively work there in the latter half of '91 as a member of the executive board of the Party For Democratic Action in Vitez and one of the vice-chairmen of the executive board of the Party for Democratic Action in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Until that time, had you been involved actively in politics before at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As vice-chairman, did you have the duty of standing in for the president or chairman in his absence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidentally, the transcript omits the answer "no" for what I think we all heard as a negative at page 16, line 7. But what was the focus of your interest at that stage in political activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Party of Democratic Action?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Within that, was there an organisation called Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Upon the initiative of the executive board of the SDA party, a humanitarian organisation of the Muslims of Vitez was formed called Merhamet, as well as the cultural society of the Muslims of Vitez called Preporod or Rebirth, of which I was also the vice-president. I was the vice-president of Merhamet and of Preporod or Rebirth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did those organisations take some of your time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I worked as a doctor in Vitez and as a doctor in the internal medicine ward in the hospital in Travnik, and in my free time, as a volunteer, I engaged in these other activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Until 1991, what had the relations between the different ethnic groups in Vitez been like? Had they been unhappy or happy or a mixture? You tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, in Vitez, in 1991, as the elections had taken place in November 1990, a new municipal parliament had been formed. I was not a member or a deputy in that parliament, which means that I didn't attend, but I was a member of the executive board of the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you're misunderstanding my question, so I'm going to cut you short, and it's my fault. Forget about politics just for the time being. Generally in Vitez, until 1990, 1991, in your experience how had the different ethnic groups got on, one with another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no major problems. As far as I know, there were no big problems in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any friction between the groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was tension because there was a war going on in Croatia. We also had some refugees from Croatia, Eastern Croatia. It was tense, in view of the fact that in the neighbourhood, there was a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But before the war, what had relations been like between the different ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had been working in Vitez since September 1979. I was frequently in a position to attend investigations, on-site investigations, in the case of traffic accidents, together with inspectors, and I do not know of a single case of any kind of conflict between members of various ethnic groups in Vitez, because in Vitez there were Croats, Serbs, Muslims, Slovenians, Macedonians. There were people from all over Yugoslavia living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any pattern of mixed marriage, that is, marriage by people of different ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We return then to matters of politics in the administration of Vitez. Following the November 1990 elections, the municipal parliament or assembly, did it have a total of some 60 delegates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And were the seats held as follows: HDZ, 23; SDA, 16; Serbians Democratic, --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- two; League of Communists, nine; Reformist party, seven; Democratic Union of Socialist Youths, two; Democratic Union of Socialists, one, or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Democratic Union had one deputy; the Socialist Youth Alliance had two, and the Democratic Socialist Alliance, one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first president of the assembly, was that Ivan Santic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did the assembly have authority over the various levels of municipal government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the highest-level body of authority in Vitez, so it did have competence over all walks of life in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The government itself, or the executive board as I think it may have been called, was that chaired by Faud Kaknjo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The executive council was the executive body of the municipal assembly, and its president was Faud Kaknjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so the chairman of the assembly, Ivan Santic, was a Croat. The chairman of the executive board, Kaknjo, was he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As you said at the beginning, you were no part of the assembly or, indeed, of the government. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, Valenta was chairman of the party until sometime in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was president of the party until mid-1992, but I'm not sure of the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In any event, when he ceased to be president, did Pero Skopljak become president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you first aware of the existence of something called Herceg-Bosna at some stage in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first heard of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in November 1991. The SDA deputies told us about it at a meeting of the executive board of the SDA party in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you later told about it by Mr. Santic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I heard it from the deputies. They asked Mr. Ivan Santic what "Herceg-Bosna" meant, and his answer was, in those days, was that it was a cultural community of Croats which was not a threat to other peoples or to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the creation of Herceg-Bosna change the atmosphere in Vitez at all at that stage or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, the first problems actually arose in Vitez at that time; first, quite insignificant, but in time they gained in intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What sort of problems then at that early stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the proposal of representatives of the HDZ, a crisis staff was formed in Vitez. I became a member of that crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to the crisis staff in a minute. Just if you can in a sentence or so, particularise the difficulties that flowed between November '91 and February of '92 from this creation of Herceg-Bosna. Can you give any examples, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. In the municipal assembly, the question was addressed to the chairperson as to what the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was. Reports were coming in from the ground that the Croatian people were being armed at an accelerated pace, and this was denied by the chief of police in Vitez, Miro Skopljak, at the assembly meeting. I heard about this from deputies at a meeting of the executive board of the SDA. He said that these were fabrications. At that time, a company was formed in Vitez called Vitez Trade, mostly composed of representatives of the HDZ, and it exported from Vitez explosives and gunpowder, and as far as we heard and saw, it was importing from Croatia weapons, bringing in money. In those days, we called it Mosunjke. This money was distributed among the Croats. And in that period, there was also a killing in the village of Zvizda. A Serb was killed. Cvijan Mijatovic was his name. In another village, Tolovici in Vitez municipality, this village was inhabited two thirds with Serbs and one third Muslims, and there were incidents between the villages of Preocica and the village of Tolovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were any of these events linked, in your mind or in the discussion of other Muslims, with the formation of Herceg-Bosna or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, we didn't believe it, but unfortunately it turned out to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move, then, to the crisis committee that you had started to tell us about, formed in the spring of 1992. What was the date on which it was formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was formed in the spring, perhaps February or March. I don't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why? Why was it formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Upon the proposal of a representative of the HDZ, because of the very serious situation and the immediate threat of war. And the purpose of the crisis staff was to assume the duties of the municipal assembly. I became a member of the crisis staff, in charge of the formation of the medical service under wartime or extraordinary conditions. My assistant was Bruno Buzuk, a doctor, a dentist, work in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thereafter, how regularly did the crisis staff meet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The crisis staff met very frequently, and the president of the crisis staff was Ivan Santic. His deputy was Faud Kaknjo. Depending on the need, they would convene the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, I'm not going to ask you to list all the members. You've done so in the past and can, no doubt, list members, if asked. But is it right that the crisis staff was expanded from politicians to include representatives of industries and factories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had, in Vitez, two crisis staffs. One was at the level of the Vitez municipality, and another was at the level of chemical factories in Vitez. I was a member of both of these crisis staffs. The chairman and deputy of the municipal crisis staffs would convene people to attend from public life, the economy, politics, individuals they thought would be helpful in dealing with certain problems as they arose. But the permanent members were 10, and the others would be occasionally invited to attend. I don't know whether later on the managers of these factories became full-fledged members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this early stage of the crisis staff, were the various ethnic groups working together in harmony or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For how long did the crisis staff operate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The crisis staff, as far as I can recall, operated from mid-March, or maybe February, until mid-June. It operated -- actually, it acted in line with the purpose for which it was formed. That is, it had the competencies of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come to the end of that period in June, let me deal with -- or I'll let you deal with a couple of events happening in May. First, simply as an example of the documentation that was raised, Exhibit 103, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before this document is distributed, the number is incorrect, but perhaps if we can change it by hand to "103.1", that will solve the problem. It's not listed in our list of exhibits for reasons that will become clear. May the witness have one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we appear to be venturing into matters in controversy now, so I think it might make some sense for the Prosecution to proceed by way of normal rules of direct examination rather than leading questions. They invited us to make an observation at the appropriate point, and I think this is the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document, in the copy I have, has the original on one side and the English version on the other. If you would just look, please, at the original B/C/S version, "Yes" or "No", does this appear to you to be the photocopy of a genuine document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is not signed, but otherwise, I think it is. Mention is made of my name here, which means I was present at the crisis staff meeting held on the 12th of May, 1992, and at that time I was given specific assignments. I can explain which they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We need only look at item number 4, which says that, "Dr. Mujezinovic is charged with delivering to the Vitez Medical Centre a part of the supply of antibiotics from the available medical supplies." Was that indeed one of the duties that was imposed on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I already said that I was charged with forming the medical service under wartime conditions. In the chemical factories in Vitez, we had quite a large quantity of medical supplies, because their production was in this line of work, and this was the material for which Mario Cerkez was in charge, and I was given instruction that I should take medical supplies from the SDS, and together with Bruno Buzuk that we should distribute it throughout the network of outpatient clinics in the field. Most of that material was to have been given to the medical centre in Vitez, or its reserve location in the event of war, and at the motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's at the moment, I think, all I want. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into private session, just for about three questions? It relates to the topic I raised earlier this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there one meeting in the period March to June of 1992, one meeting of the crisis staff, where Anto Valenta said something that you can remember particularly about the future?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the end of April 1992, at one of the crisis staff meetings, towards the very end of it, Anto Valenta, who was then president of the HDZ for Vitez, said in passing to us that the Muslims of Vitez and the others must place themselves under the command of the HVO, and that they must accept that, because he said that in Vitez at the time the HVO of Vitez was 90 per cent armed, that according to his assessment, the Muslims were armed 10 per cent. He also mentioned the HOS, which was operating in Vitez. He said that the HOS had no importance for the HVO. At the time, we couldn't believe this. What is more, the chairman, Ivan Santic, said, "Come on, Anto, you always complicate things." And his answer was, "No, I'm not joking. You just think this over."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The HVO, when had you first been aware of that, as a body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learnt about the HVO in the first half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you first learnt of it, what was it? What did it do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a military formation in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the time that Valenta said what you've described his saying, was it just a military organisation, or had it started to assume other responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, it was only a military formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so in light of what was said by Santic and about him by his colleague, did you take what he said seriously, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to tell you quite honestly, we were very worried, that would be perhaps the best word, because at that time, we were agreeing together, or rather took a decision at the crisis staff to take away the weapons from the former army, the JNA, because those weapons were the property of the Territorial Defence, and the former army had taken it away and stored it in its base in a village called Slimena, near Travnik. So the crisis committee decided that the TO, the HVO, should together take away those weapons. I was the medical security. I believe it was done on the 4th of May, '92. But we were very worried by Anto Valenta's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was your initial reaction that you should do what he proposed, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We thought right at the beginning -- I mean, that question was raised at the SDA executive board. We thought we should not place ourselves under the command of the HVO. We thought we should have a joint Defence force. We thought we even suggested that the commander of these joint armed forces in Vitez be Mr. Franjo Petrac. We did not object to having a Croat as the joint commander of the TO and HVO at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next topic, the murder of somebody called Samir Trako: Can you help us with that? When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It happened sometime around the 20th of May, '92, in the late hours. Well, generally speaking, the chairman of the crisis staff, Mr. Santic, called me and asked me to come urgently to a meeting of the crisis staff in his office. He did not tell me the reason. So I went there, and in his office, other members of the crisis staff were present, and Mario Cerkez was also there, sitting, when Mr. Ivan Santic explained to us why he had called us to the crisis staff. He said that an unpleasant incident had happened, that a TO member had been killed, that two had been arrested, and called upon all of us to prevail upon people in the town to calm the situation down. Then the floor was taken by Cerkez, by Mario Cerkez, who at that time was the HVO commander, the commander of the HVO staff in Vitez, and he explained the circumstances under which that thing happened. He seemed to me under the influence of alcohol. He said that three young men had come to the brewery in the basement of the hotel, that they sat at the bar, that they behaved very provocatively, that they asked for drinks, and that at the exit from the hotel, that they also challenged Miro Vukadinovic, an HVO guard, and that he fired at one of them, and that he was then killed, and that the HVO military police arrested the other two. The crisis staff then decided to conduct an investigation and that the two arrested soldiers of the Territorial Defence from Vitez be handed over to the military police of the Territorial Defence in Vitez. It was also decided that a team should go and notify the family that that young man had been killed. I was on that team, also the police commander, Saban Mahmutovic, Fuad Kaknjo as the deputy chairman of the crisis staff, and at that time I offered even Santic to join us because he also enjoyed great prestige in Vitez, but he refused and said that we, the Muslims, should solve it amongst ourselves. Mario Cerkez telephoned from the office and ordered to hand over the two arrested to the TO military police and promised that they would be brought and turned over straight away. Fuad Kaknjo, Saban Mahmutovic, and I were in front of the building waiting for the HVO military police to bring those two arrested soldiers. We waited for an hour, and they still did not turn up in front of the hotel. I saw Ivan Budimir, who was the commander of the military police, the Croatian Defence Council, in Vitez, and I went to ask him why those arrested TO members weren't coming. He told me, "Doctor, I called twice. There's a hitch somewhere. Something is happening." I knew Ivan Budimir very well, because he was the coach of the football team in Vitez, and I was the deputy chairman of the club board. So I asked him, "How could that happen?" And he told me, "Doctor, don't you see that Mario is drunk? He came after those young men, from the hotel after those young men and fired a shot at the last one. We did all we could to save him, but unfortunately he was dead. We transferred him to the Travnik hospital by our vehicle, but he was dead." He promised that he would still insist on releasing the two arrested ones. After that, we went to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt. Doctor, you've been speaking for some time, and we need --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge May, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Doctor, you've been speaking for some time, and we need a pause for a moment. You suggest, in speaking to Budimir, you asked, "How could that happen?" And he said, "Don't you see that Mario is drunk? He came after those young men from the hotel and fired a shot at the last one. We did what we could to save him, but unfortunately he was dead." Mr. Nice, I wonder if you could clarify that passage, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Incidentally, with witnesses like this witness, where the long narrative answer is the material, but in the event I want, I'm not going to interrupt him, because it only takes time. So it was a long answer, but in fact he was covering the territory that I wanted him to cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, just clarify, please, though, that last part of your account. Ivan Budimir was telling you something in answer to what question? What were you really-- what did you ask him, first of all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked Ivan Budimir how did the incident happen, how did it come about, how the man was killed. And he answered, "Didn't you realise, Doctor, that Mario was drunk? When those young men were coming out from the hotel, he followed them and fired at the last one." I'm only conveying the words of Ivan Budimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long before your meeting with Mario Cerkez did you understand that the death had occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learnt about it at the meeting itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment, Doctor; there's an objection. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're on the brink of hearsay right now, and will you ask the Prosecutor, so as not to waste more time later, will you ask the Prosecutor to ask the witness if the mentioned Budimir is alive or not and about his whereabouts, so that we could have confirmed the information mentioned by the witness. Only then can we really decide whether it is hearsay or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know that one follows from the other, but I'm certainly happy to ask the witness whether he knows where Ivan Budimir is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know if Ivan Budimir is alive or dead, Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About four months ago, I learnt that Ivan Budimir was no longer alive. I learnt it from my medical assistant, Franjo Petrac, that he had been killed in the village of Mosunj. So I asked about Ivan Budimir, Franjo Petrac, the chief medical technician in Vitez, in the health centre, because he was an associate of mine, and I repeated; he told me, "No, unfortunately, he is no longer with us." I did not know that before that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When, apparently, did he die? When was he killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And before I come back to the topic of the conversation that we were most recently dealing with, what sort of man was Ivan Budimir? What was his job, what was he like as a man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked together with Ivan Budimir in the football club, and he was a very hardworking man, a man who taught children football. He was a coach. For some time he was the chief coach of the soccer club, and for a while he was assistant coach. For instance, when I voted who the coach would be, I always voted for him, because he was a serious and hardworking man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity, to use that word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And how was he regarded generally in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vitez, before the war and during the war, I think -- I believe people trusted him, because they knew him. You know, it's a small place, and everybody knows the coach of the football team. The football team, of course, had all the ethnicities represented, and he was coaching them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And how did he die?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Back to the question I was asking you: You went to this meeting, and you saw Cerkez. You were informed of the death of Trako. Were you told how long before the meeting Trako had died, had been killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't told that. All I was told was that an incident had taken place, and, as I said before, the time was not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you noticed Cerkez's condition at the meeting as being one where he was affected by alcohol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was how he looked to me, at least. It seemed to me that he was affected by alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What signs was he showing, if you can recall at this remove of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Mario Cerkez very well, and here he was very garrulous, his face was flushed, and as soon as we asked to have those two released, he immediately took up the telephone -- he has this mobile one -- and called -- I mean, I did not know that Mario Cerkez before. Formerly he was very nice, and we often would have coffee together at the factory compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm sorry to interrupt you; there's a matter I want to raise with counsel, and I've raised it with my colleagues. What is the relevance of this evidence? It's clearly prejudicial as far as Mr. Cerkez is concerned. As far as I recollect, there is no account in which this murder appears.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, absolutely right, but it's plainly of value both in relation to disposition as to Muslims generally, and, indeed, as to his disposition generally, which may come up for argument and consideration later, when the matters more specifically charged are to be dealt with. So it's plainly relevant, and we would invite the Tribunal to carry on hearing the comparatively limited evidence, limited in terms of time, that will touch upon it. So far as this witness is concerned, I have only two more questions to ask which tie it in with earlier evidence given by, I think, the last witness or the last witness but one. Then we'll be done with this topic, and I'll move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not the length which concerns me, the length of the answers; it's whether it's relevant or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the victim of course was a Muslim. We are dealing here with the developing state of thinking and the developing attitudes of the parties. In due course, the Tribunal will be concerned with the control of Cerkez, the discipline by Cerkez of subordinates, and in relation to all of those matters, this evidence may be very powerful evidence indeed. In any event, it's now before the Court, and I would respectfully invite you to -- well, I'll leave it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As Your Honour notes, the danger of bad character evidence against Mr. Cerkez is obvious, and to the extent that we are going to be tagged in some fashion with command, control, conspiracy, unity, co-defendants, our association with someone whose character is being assassinated, while peripheral, is still a concern to us. So I suggest again, since this is an unindicted, uncharged crime now attempted to be proved circumstantially through a witness who is deceased, and there's no direct linkage, its attenuation versus its prejudicial effect is so clear it ought not to be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I just add one point in relation to that: Of course, the evidence shows not only the killing, but it also shows the ability to control due judicial process at the time. It was to this, of course, that Zlotrg's evidence was particularly relevant, and the last two questions I would ask of this witness would touch on that same point: What happened, or to be precise, what did not happen afterwards? On issues of command and control generally, and on wider issues, the question whether these defendants, singularly or as part of a collective body bearing responsibility, obeyed rules or bent rules to suit themselves, even at this early stage, is plainly of potential value. It shows the scale of control they had and their willingness to abuse it, and it's not material that can be properly overlooked, in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we will admit the evidence, but on a limited basis. We think it has some relevance -- or may have some relevance; it's too early to say -- as part of the background and as part of the evidence relating to command and control. We do not accept it as evidence of bad character, and we bear in mind and disregard that aspect of the evidence. We also bear in mind that, of course, it's hearsay evidence again. We'll have to decide what weight, if any, it has. Perhaps you could finish it fairly briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I just want to add this: One of the concerns of the Trial Chamber is that we don't get bogged down, if I can put it that way, in detail about individual events. I think I've raised this in relation to this particular event when evidence was given about it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two other questions, please, Dr. Mujezinovic. First, was there an investigation ordered into this death; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it, to your knowledge, ever completed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the man named Vukadinovic ever brought back to Vitez, or indeed ever heard of again in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We raised that question. We asked about Miro Vukadinovic, and at the crisis staff we were told that he had disappeared from Vitez. The investigation was conducted in Vitez. Vlado Miskovic, the prosecutor in district court in Travnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard something about this before, and I'm going to move on. You told us that the crisis staff only survived until June of 1992. What brought the crisis staff to an end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometime in mid-June, the building of the municipal hall and the civilian police was taken over by HVO soldiers. They disarmed policemen of Muslim ethnicity, and they kept the building for about three days. At the time, we did not know what it was all about. The chairman of the crisis staff convened a meeting three or four days later and said that he did not support that kind of methods, this forcible take-over of buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were flags raised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The flags of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian state, were hoisted above those buildings. At that meeting, Anto Valenta made a comment, saying that this had been done by armed groups not controlled by the HDZ. Pero Skopljak said that it had been done by people who could no longer wait, because the Croat people were awaiting change, and Ivan Santic, who they class worked in the municipal hall and as civilian policeman, to come -- I mean Muslims, to come back to work. On that occasion, he informed that the HVO government had been formed in Vitez and asked a Muslim representative that the officials of Muslim nationality place themselves under the authority of the newly-formed Croatian authority in Vitez. He said that the HVO government had decided that Vitez was to become part of the union of communities, of municipal communities within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and that the BH army or, rather, [indiscernible] In Vitez be also placed under the command of the HVO staff in Vitez. And he also requested that the civilian policemen of Muslim ethnicity work for the civilian police of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna and pursuant to rules and decrees of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. Mumib Kaimovic was talking over this, who took part in a discussion at that meeting, and I can tell you briefly what they thought and what they said; that this was an attack against lawful bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, were Muslims prepared to join in with the HVO government, as suggested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that meeting, that was the first time that we heard of the HVO government in Vitez, and we took part in the discussion. When we were invited there, it was as members of the crisis staff of the municipality of Vitez, and at that time -- I didn't really understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were Muslims prepared to take part in what was happening, or what was their attitude to what you were being told?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. At that time, they were not really ready to accept it. To begin with, they had no jurisdiction for that. They said it was an attack against lawful authorities, that this was breach of sovereignty of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that it looked like the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they did not take a firm stand at that particular meeting. They refused this --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll cut you short again. Two short questions. You told us, I think, about the Muslim police being relieved of their weapons. Were their weapons returned to them, and were they able to resume their jobs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, later they were returned those weapons, and they returned to the joint civilian police and were there until October '92. There was the joint civilian police in Vitez, that is, made of Muslims, Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A second short question. At about this time, were you receiving any personal advice, yourself, or any personal warnings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992, at that time I personally did not receive any advice. I worked for the health centre and in Travnik, and here I was present as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a soldier you knew called by the name of Miro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Miro? Yes, but -- Miro Saric, Miro Vukadinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know the man. I didn't know the man. No, I did not. I know the Vukadinovic family, I know some of them who live in the village of Kruscica. But him, no, I did not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if the Chamber is looking for a time, but I see the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now. Half an hour. For "half an hour", read 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Staying with the middle of 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Staying in the middle of 1992, Dr. Mujezinovic, just to see if you can help us with any statements by any other of the named persons in whom we have an interest. Skopljak, did he say anything at about that time, that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are several Skopljaks in Vitez. I don't know who you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pero.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pero Skopljak was the president or, rather, the head of the civilian police in Vitez until '91 and in the first half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the first half of 1992, did he say anything about the future, that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pero Skopljak was also a member of the crisis staff of Vitez municipality. I have already stated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Counsel Nice, I think the Chamber has a problem with the way this witness is being interrogated. You are asking him to say something about the future. We can't -- you can't talk about the future as much as you want in a narrative. But these are not questions that are normally being asked in a criminal trial. You have to narrow down to focus on the events in the indictment, and that is the way you can control the procedure. Thank you for taking this into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I quite understand that, but in fact the questions I'm asking, in a non-leading form, are questions as to what, if anything, was said by the names in whom we have an interest at the time about what was to come. But if the witness is unable to help us in relation to the name I've just given --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you at the time, in the middle of 1992, did you know the name Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met Dario Kordic in the first half of 1992. Before that, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he, in the first half of 1992 or in the middle, either personally or on the television or the radio, say anything about what was happening or what was to come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember for the first half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I simply cannot remember these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Well, then let's move, finally, to Mario Cerkez. You spoke earlier on of his being the HVO staff commander and also as the HVO commander. Was there any difference or was that the same, so far as you were concerned, staff commander and commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I was using it synonymously. I think it is the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. He was present at talks in the first half of 1992. I think you may have said this already. What, if anything, did he say about the abilities of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From that time period, the first half of 1992, as I already said, I only heard from Anto Valenta what the ability of the HVO in Vitez were. In that period, I really didn't hear anything from Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we deal with something called HOS? You've mentioned it already, and you can deal with it really quite shortly, certainly at the moment. What was HOS and when were you first aware of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HOS, in Vitez, was a military organisation of the Croatian Party of Rights. There was a unit in Vitez, the commander of which was Darko Kraljevic. It operated, I think, at the end of '91 and the first half of 1992 in Vitez under the name of HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The man Darko Kraljevic, did you have quite a lot to do with him for particular reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't frequently come across Darko Kraljevic, but on one occasion I was sitting with his father when he approached our table and had a chat with us. A second time I met Kraljevic, he was sick, but otherwise I didn't have any special contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, the witness mentioned HOS. I have the transcript here in English, "in Vitez, was a military organisation of the Croatian Party of Rights", which was not well translated into French. The Croat Party of Rights, I suppose civil rights or human rights. What is that party? Could we ask the witness, what is that party, that Croatian Party of Rights which he said was the party apparently supervising the activities of HOS? So HOS would be the military arm of the Party of Rights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) What is the Croatian Party of Rights? Could the witness tell us about that party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That party, in Vitez, did not take part in the parliamentary elections in 1990. It emerged later on. It was the extended arm of the Croatian Party of Rights from Croatia, headed by a man called Paraga, as far as I can recollect, like the HDZ. So the Croatian Party of Rights were branches of the Croatian parties in Croatia of the same name. They had a military arm called HOS and which, in Vitez, had its own area. It was well armed. I don't know how strong it was, how many members it had. But as I said, the commander of the HOS was Darko Kraljevic, and the president of the Croatian Party of Rights in Vitez was a certain man called Franjo Krizanac, also known as Paraga.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This party, was it a right-wing, a left-wing, a centrist, a reformist party, if it can be categorised in that way? Or alternatively say it can't be so categorised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, that party, according to its programme, fought for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, as far as I know. I'm not very familiar with it. And the president of the Party of Rights offered, on two or three occasions, closer cooperation with the SDA in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Darko Kraljevic was unwell, I think you said; tell us about that. In what way was he unwell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked on a regular basis in Vitez as a physician. One morning I came to work, and I had coffee with my colleagues, Dr. Franjo Tibold from Vitez, and Zvonko Kajic. They left the room we were sitting in, and about an hour later they came back and asked me to go to Darko Kraljevic. I simply said, "I feel awkward." They said that Darko Kraljevic had had a heart attack, and they wanted me to examine him. So I went with them. His men drove us there, to a building of the Sumarija, the forestry company in Vitez, in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Taking the story shortly, when you examined him, what possible diagnosis did you make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see any signs of an infarction. There was tachycardia. He was angry, he was aggressive, and I gave him a shot for detoxification from alcohol, one in his vein and another intramuscular. I gave him diazepam, and after ten or fifteen minutes, Darko started to curse and to insult my colleagues, Croats. He said, "You see, I'm feeling well now; how come you couldn't treat me like that?" After that, Darko would come to see me at home, under escort, in civilian clothes, he came to my home. And I had to stand in front of the surgery when the nurse was giving Darko Kraljevic a shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why was he being given injections? For what condition? I want to deal with this quite quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suspected that he was intoxicated by alcohol or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the other substance might have been ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suspected intoxication.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of your encounters with Darko Kraljevic, did he tell you about what he was doing and what he was being expected to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the course of these sessions when he was having injections, very often his wife was with him, and he would say to me that Pero Skopljak, Anto Valenta, Mario Cerkez, were trying to persuade him to place himself under the command of the HVO, that he had to wage war against the Muslims -- or rather that he should mistreat the Muslims. He told me then that he would not agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say "mistreat the Muslims," was he specific as to what was expected of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To break into houses of the prestigious individuals, that a kind of intimidation that the Muslims of Vitez should be got going.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as to children and women, what, if anything, were his instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- no, actually, I already said what he told me. Children, women, individuals of prestige, that his unit, his soldiers, wanted him to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, Mr. President, I should like to object once again on the same grounds. The witness is mentioning as a source something that Kraljevic said, and for us to be able to see to what extent this is direct knowledge or rather hearsay, I should like to ask my learned friend, the Prosecutor, to ask the witness whether Darko Kraljevic is alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No problem with that. Again, we were going to come to it in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Kraljevic: Alive, or dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I have heard, Kraljevic was killed after the war in a traffic accident. That is what I heard. It was -- at the entrance to Vitez, there is a monument to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Back, then, to what you were being told by Kraljevic -- and it was for this reason I wanted you to tell us a bit more about his condition -- at the times he was saying these things to you, how lucid, how clear did he appear to be in his mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, at that time he told me that he wouldn't accept it, that he was thinking of leaving Bosna with his family. His family came from Herzegovina. I was extremely surprised when I later saw Kraljevic on television as a colonel, as a commander of the military unit known as Vitezovi, in view of what he said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come to the Vitezovi later, but my question to you was: How clear was he in his mind when he told you what was being asked of him by others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, he seemed to me to be quite okay. He wasn't aggressive. He spoke to me in a normal tone of voice. I was sitting in the car next to him. He wasn't shouting; he wasn't aggressive. It was a normal kind of conversation, under normal conditions, the way people talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: HOS survived as a group until when? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I think in the second half of '92 they were operating in Vitez as a military unit of the HVO called Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Kraljevic, was he in some way involved with the Vitezovi, and if so, in what way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was introduced on the media as the commander of the military unit, the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's turn now to the coordination committee for the protection of Muslims. Can you tell us, please, how it came about that that body was formed, and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The coordination committee for the protection of Muslims in Vitez was founded in the first half of July. In view of the fact that a one-nation HVO government had been proclaimed in Vitez, that in fact the legal authorities had been toppled, upon the initiative of the executive board of the SDA of Vitez, the president, Munir Kajmovic, invited prominent Muslims in Vitez and other representatives of parties, because only 60 per cent of the Muslims had voted for the SDA whereas 40 per cent of the Muslims had voted for other parties, and we felt that we could not take decisions on behalf of all the Muslims of Vitez. At the meeting, it was agreed that a body be set up which we called the coordination committee for the protection of Muslims. It numbered 19 members. The president of the coordination committee for the protection of Muslims of Vitez was Fuad Kaknjo, the president of the executive board of Vitez municipality. At that meeting, decisions were taken --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And again, I want to deal with it comparatively swiftly: Was this committee in any senses a government or parallel government, or was its function different from that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Its function was not that of a government, but rather to monitor in Vitez all walks of life with respect to any violations of the interests and rights of Muslims in Vitez, and to address the public through the media telling them where the rights and interests of the Muslims had been violated. We gave instructions that Fuad Kaknjo, as president of the executive council, should continue working in the executive council as the legal government in Vitez municipality. That was our conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the overall objectives of this committee were to do what for life in Vitez, as its real aims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To draw the attention of the public to the forcible imposition of government in Vitez by a single ethnic community, and to brief the public as to what that government was doing in Vitez, how it was operating, because the newly formed government was exclusive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 210, please. Double-sided for the Court and for the Defence, but two sheets for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this a press release that went out -- I'm sorry about the quality of the copy, but is it a press release that went out on the 10th of September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Headed "Co-ordination Board for the Protection of Muslims' Interests," within the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Vitez Municipality, and it sets out here complaint or outrage at a decision, in particular: "According to the decision of the so-called Croatian Defence Council ... of 3 September 1992 it has been decided that instruction in elementary and secondary schools in the municipality ..." should involve school books published in Croatia, and various other provisions -- again, in accordance with last week's practice, I don't need to read the document in detail unless the Chamber wants me to -- and the coordination board set out its outrage at this decision and set out its reasons why. In the second-to-last paragraph, it called on the citizens not to respect the decision because it's to the detriment of the non-Croatian population, and said that instruction -- that is, instruction in schools -- would not start on the established date, and said that this was another example of the so-called democracy in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Before we turn from this committee, how effective was it, Dr. Mujezinovic, this committee, in your judgement? What did it achieve, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That coordinating committee for the protection of Muslims, apart from taking note of the violations of rights and interests, and apart from continuing our coordination with HDZ members, sometime in August we managed to bring together the main staff of the Vitez HDZ and Vitez SDA to convene their meeting and try to see if we could solve, jointly, problems in Vitez. At that meeting, we agreed that in Vitez we should call the government the Muslim/Croat Defence Council, because there were all the Croats and Muslims in Vitez represented there. That suggestion was made by Josip Silic, a Croat from Vitez. We were all happy that a compromise had been found, and some three or four days later Munib Kajmovic, as the president of the SDA at Vitez, told us at the executive board that Anto Valenta now, as the deputy president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, told him that nothing would come out of it because they had not been given the green light from Grude.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By "Grude," you mean -- or by "Grude," he meant ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Grude is where, from what we knew, was the seat of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So even at this stage, were you pressing for co-operation with Croats in the HDZ, or were you pressing for separation of interests and powers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, all the time we kept in touch and were looking for a compromise to, set up a joint authority in Vitez and to set up a joint military command and joint police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I turn to topic 9 on my little schedule, I'll just deal with topic 10 and then come back: Refugees, please. What was the position so far as refugees in Vitez were concerned? Were there refugees, where were they coming from, when did they first start to arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vitez, there were refugees. First refugees from Croatia began to arrive; that is in '91, from Vukovar, from Sid. But there were not many of them, and largely they came to stay with their relatives in Vitez. There were some sick people and elderly. Subsequently, a large number of refugees arrived from West and East Bosnia, mostly of Muslim ethnicity. As far as I can recall, sometime in September or October, there were over 4.000 Muslim refugees in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where were they living, for the most part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some were staying with relations, that is, if they had relations there. Others were accommodated in weekend cottages and summer cottages of Zenica inhabitants. In Vitez, that is in the locality of Ahmici and Kruscica, there were very many summer cottages, and these people either stayed with their relations or in those cottages in Kruscica and Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the accommodation in those summer cottages organised by any particular body, and if so, how did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the accommodation was organised in the second half -- that is, I think, in October, November, and December, it was Mehmed Ahmic who was in charge of that, and we suggested to him that he ask the owners to turn him over the keys in order to accommodate those unfortunate people who arrived with a couple of bags or rather with nothing at all. We had Merhamet in Vitez, and through Merhamet we distributed food among them, and clothing, and some footwear, and money, when there was some. I had 20 refugees at home in my own house for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How, generally, did the refugees behave? And I don't think you've yet given us date for when they first started to arrive, if you can help us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The refugees began to arrive sometime in mid '92, Muslims, that is, and I said that Croats arrived from Croatia in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And how did the Muslim refugees behave, generally, in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not heard that they caused trouble in Vitez. I did not hear any such thing. They were happy that they were being put up somewhere, that they were being given food or clothes. They asked for more always, but we gave them as much as we could. At that time we were cooperating with the UNHCR, with the International Red Cross, nongovernmental organisations which operated in Bosnia at the time, and were given food, clothing, footwear by them, and through Merhamet we distributed those items. We had a whole service set up which kept record of who had arrived, where he had been accommodated, what he had been issued and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they, as far as you could judge, generate any ethnic discord in the community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion -- and I was the vice-chairman of the Merhamet charitable organisation in Vitez; we also had a pharmacy -- and I heard on the local Croat television, I heard a gentleman who unfortunately is no longer alive, Anto Marijanovic, and he was at the time the editor, that Muslims were pursuing a cunning policy whereby they were setting out to change the demographic structure of the Vitez municipality so that they could win power in Vitez at the next elections. I was appalled by that, and I asked him, "Anto, how can you say that?" And he said, "Well, we have to say something." I mean, it did not depend on Muslims in Vitez, how many of them we would receive, how many of them we could receive. They were asking for help. And in the first half --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll cut you short there, because I want to move from the refugees coming to Vitez to the movement of Muslims from Vitez: When did the process of Muslims leaving Vitez begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, at a Merhamet meeting, the secretary who was keeping the record, in the presence of officers of the International Red Cross from France, she said sometime around the 10th of April, '93, three or four hundred refugees had suddenly left Vitez, and a large scale departure of Muslims from Vitez, or rather the expulsion of Muslims from Vitez, began on the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. So far as humanitarian aid was concerned for refugees, was that humanitarian aid always available to them, or did there come a time when for any reason it stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions which existed for the reception of refugees, one of the conditions was that they all had to report to the Red Cross in Vitez. Sometime in November '92, the HVO government simply prohibited the work of the Red Cross, prohibited Suad Caic, who was the president of the Red Cross, and his typist, to enter there. They seized the seals, and we could not any longer make record of Muslim refugees in Vitez, because from that card, from that application, the application of the Red Cross was the basis on which we could receive aid from international organisations. At the same time, Mehmed Ahmic, who was responsible for putting up, for accommodating refugees, informed us that Dario Kordic had prohibited the settlement of refugees in the municipality in Busovaca at that period of time. So we found ourselves in a rather embarrassing position. And then the refugees began to slowly -- I mean refugees of Muslim ethnicity -- began slowly to leave Vitez. I think we have records.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And when was this announcement by Dario Kordic, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one of the Merhamet meetings, I think it was sometime in November '92, but I am transmitting to you the man in charge of the matter was the one who told us that, at the meeting, and his name was Mehmed Ahmic, called Sudzuka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I now want to deal generally with the period June '92 to January '93, topic 9, and with what happened so far as Muslim buildings, businesses, and so on, were concerned. In that period, was there a change in the life of Muslims in the town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time when the HVO appointed Vitez government, I already said that money was arriving from Croatia, the money that was not being used in Croatia anymore. Then weapons arrived. Those weapons were also sold to Muslims. The first attack, I mean physical attack, against local Muslims in Vitez began sometime around the 10th of September, when the SDA kiosk in Vitez was destroyed, that is, the lottery of the SDA in Vitez. Then the bust of a national hero, a national hero of the last world war, was also demolished sometime around the 20th. Then I think it was around the 20th of October when the HVO attacked TO units in Vitez, and then the command post of the TO was taken, the logistics of the TO was taken over. And then in Ahmici four houses were destroyed, then farm buildings, about 20 buildings were damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before you move too far forward, just because you haven't dealt with it in detail, the kiosk that you've referred to and the national hero whose bust was destroyed, did either of them have Muslim connections or was the kiosk Muslim owned or not and was the hero a Muslim or not, just so we can know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The kiosk belonged to the SDA party, and the bust, the man's name was Mosa Pijade, and he was of Jewish origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Picking it up at about the 20th or, more precisely, maybe the 21st of October, were you working in the hospital on the 21st of October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that weekend, I was working in the hospital. I was on duty there. On the 19th, I worked in Vitez and I learned, on the morning of the 20th, that there had been a conflict in the village of Ahmici between TO and HVO members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see any of the victims or people who were apparently victims of that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and since we had moved the health centre to a reserve site from Vitez, rather from the urban part of Vitez, wounded people came to us, mostly Muslims. But they also brought to us a man from Ahmici with his elbows smashed. I think his name was Nesib Kajmakovic. And I was at home at the time. It was lunchtime, but they called me and asked me to come back urgently. And when I came, Dr. Bruno Buzuk and Dr. Enisa Mulalic were having an argument with two or three HVO soldiers who wanted to kill that wounded man. Owing to Dr. Bruno Buzuk, we extended aid to that wounded, and he was then taken by an ambulance car to the hospital in Zenica, to the orthopaedic surgery. That day, there were five or six of them, as I said, on the 20th of October, civilian wounded who came to us, to the health centre, looking for medical help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the HVO soldiers were saying this, that they wanted to kill the man in the hospital itself, or where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They wanted to take him out into the street and kill him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Back then to the 21st of October, if your memory is such that you can take us through the important events of the next few months without my interrupting you, do so. Otherwise, I'll take you to various topics. But can you now remember the developing history so as to give us, without concentrating on minor details, just give us the major events? Can you take us through to January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try to be as concise as possible. In that period after the 21st of October, a Croat from Vitez, Ilija Safradin, approached me and told me that soldiers of the BH army had seized his car, and asked me for help. I went to the secondary school with Stipo Kristo, the driver, and in the command I found about 15 or 20 members of the BH army or, rather, the TO, and I asked to see the commander, Sefkija Djidic. Nihad Rebihic told me that he was standing in for him. I asked him where was the commander, and he said he was in Stari Vitez at the reserve command post. With the same driver, I went there and I asked Sefkija to return the car to Ilija Safradin, and he ordered a military policeman to bring that car and asked me to establish contact with Ivan Santic to try to calm down the situation and convene a meeting. When we returned, I called Ivan Santic and I said Sefkija was asking for a meeting, and he also told me that he had been issued the order by the district TO staff that a blockade should be put up on the road to Ahmici. But he said that he had very few soldiers, that all his soldiers were on the front line. He also said that the HVO would just step up, go through that blockade, and that people would die just like that. With the help of the UNHCR in Vitez and Ivan Santic, I convened that meeting, and I attended one of those meetings. I think it was on the 23rd at the joint meeting convened to appease the situation in Vitez. Together with Pero Skopljak and a local priest both of the Muslim and Croat origin, we appeared on -- we came on television. We were trying to call upon people -- we were appealing to people, telling them that there was no need for concern, that an understanding had been reached, that talks were being conducted at the level of higher commands or, rather, at the republican level, and so that the situation was rather calm for a few or three days. But then at the beginning of November, at night, about 10 buildings were blown up, and they were owned by Muslims in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What buildings were those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were restaurants or coffee shops or hairdressers, photographers, owned by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the Muslim population to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were asking, "Why, what for, how?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the answers you got, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We mostly received the same answer, that these were done by people who were not controlled by the HVO, people whom the HVO could not control. Anyway, I mean these are very vague answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And who was identified as beyond the control of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. It was really -- I could not really understand who that was, because they were mostly HVO soldiers who blew up those buildings. That was a method of intimidation of people living in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on, then, from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I want to find out who gave the answer that those activities were done by people who were not controlled by the HVO. Who is it that gave that answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We continued to be in touch with members of the crisis staff; Ivan Santic, Pero Skopljak, Anto Valenta. Also present frequently at the meetings of the crisis staff was Mario Cerkez. And mostly they were the people who represented the Croatian side in all agreements and negotiations. For example, on the 23rd and 24th of October, a motel called Plavac in Kruscica was destroyed and the guard was killed, and the motel was owned by a Muslim who was a commander of the BH army in that area. His name was Hakija Gelilovic. Towards the end of November, two soldiers were killed on the road to Kruscica, and then when the refugees from Jajce came --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Keep in mind Judge Robinson's question. He specifically wanted to know who was giving you the answer to your query about responsibility for these actions. I hope I haven't cut you short too quickly, but focus on that question of the Judge's, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember once when Anto Valenta told us at a meeting, when we asked him about these incidents, he said, "Perhaps it is being done by the Muslim extremists to deepen the rift," because we asked him, "Who is doing this?" And the answer by responsible officials of the HVO was that this was being done by people who were out of control of the HVO, and I have listed the four names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you've taken us up to the end of November, I think. Are there any important events of the type you've described that happened before the end of November, or does that pretty well conclude it until then? I know there's a bank to be dealt with, but I think that comes later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the end of November, two members of the BH army were killed on the road between Vitez and Kruscica. Also in January --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am going to stop you now because I want to introduce another exhibit. 294, please. So things can be broadly chronological, I'm going to -- in order to achieve, wherever possible, chronological development, I'm going to ask everybody to have that document in their hands, but also to have an earlier one, 246, and then they can be dealt with in the correct order. As to 246, it's my error entirely, if the witnesses could have 246 in the B/C/S first, it's 246 for which I required a minute of private session this morning. If I could have private session now, please, for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
