utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next document, Document 294, dated the 26th of November, do you have that before you, please? This is a press release dated the 26th of November, and it starts off with a reference to the fact that since the 25th of November, there hasn't been a single representative of the authorities of Muslim nationality in the building of the assembly of the Vitez municipality. Explain that, please, or explain this document, which can otherwise probably speak for itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In those days, the HVO government had introduced a new system of work, and all those who had not signed allegiance to the new government on that day, and I think it was the 25th of November, were not allowed entrance to their place of work. When we learned that, we issued this press release. This is a release of the executive board of the Party of Democratic Action in Vitez. Therefore, all of those who did not sign up to this new organisational set-up of the HVO and who were not loyal to that government lost their jobs. Until that day, the executive board of the municipal assembly, headed by Faud Kaknjo, worked in the same building as the HVO government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the document speaks for itself. Thank you for that. It speaks for itself. It deals with the fact that Muslim nationality policemen were not able to carry out their duties. It asks a rhetorical question, and it concludes by saying this: "In conclusion, we are calling upon the HVO government in Vitez to act seriously and cooperate, with the aim of creating a union which will respect the interests of all Vitez citizens, regardless of their national or political affiliation." It's a document not signed, but it's on behalf of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that conclusion and that invitation genuine, and were you still anxious, in the SDA, to cooperate in order to create a union for the interests of all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The result of this was an agreement reached around the 27th of January, 1993, to form, in Vitez, a wartime government of Vitez municipality where all would be represented --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to bring you to that in due course. But before we get there, I want you to move, again quite swiftly, through the history of events. We had left it at the end of November, possibly the beginning of December, I'm not sure, with the death of the two soldiers. Can you take us through any other events that happened in the end of November or in December? Then we'll come to the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have said enough, that all persons, regardless of ethnicity, including Muslims, were not allowed to enter and take up their jobs unless they signed a new certificate issued by the HVO government in Vitez, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake for not being clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We wanted to establish contact again to reach some kind of a compromise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think, Doctor, we're moving away from the point, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to take you back, Dr. Mujezinovic, please, to the events of violence and other changes in the life of Vitez between November '92 and January '93, and then we'll pick up the political environment in January. To get you back to the topic I want you to deal with, which is the series of events you've already covered, with the damage to businesses and shops and the motel and the killing of soldiers, what was the position so far as the commercial bank of Travnik is concerned? What currency did it deal with or deal in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It dealt with the former Yugoslav dinar, and then in Vitez, the Croatian currency was introduced. Then the Croatian curricula from Croatia, various symbols of the Croatian state. There was political pressure on the Muslims of Vitez to accept this as being the reality. In fact, Croatian authority was fully asserted, and no mention was made of others anymore. After this announcement of ours, the situation did not calm down. Shops continued to be blown up. The economic bank -- commercial bank of Travnik in Vitez was blown up. Then Zmajevac. The owner was from Zenica. Then the Klevija company based in Zavidovici. Individual Muslims were taken into custody for interrogation, physical abuse, threats, such as, for instance, engineer Suad Salkic, who was an honorary citizen of the town of Zagreb; Dr. Ridzanovic, with a PHD in technology. A well-known businessman in Vitez was killed and plundered in Stara Bila. Another businessman on the way out of Vitez in the village of Nadioci was killed. Policemen were taken into detention, policemen of Muslim ethnicity in those days, that is, in January we learned. I didn't hear it, but at our meetings, we were told that Mr. Dario Kordic had proclaimed the members of the BH army and the police as being paramilitary formations, stating that the only lawful unit within historical Croatian borders was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's time for our adjournment. We've had the contemporary notes of events made by an earlier witness as Exhibit 332.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Document 11 does come next on my list, and we're moving on to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but we don't want repeated those allegations with which we've already dealt, unless there's been a challenge to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm satisfied that we will conclude this witness in chief this afternoon, and I mentioned earlier the possibility of -- this has nothing to do with the evidence of this witness, but I just mentioned the possibility this morning of another witness being available to make sure that the balance of the week will be filled with evidence. Providing there's enough of the week at the end of it to take that witness, he's able to come, I'm happy to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sure that's the case, that you've got all those matters in mind, Mr. Nice, but I'm just saying that we, because I'm reminded of it and now I look to it, Exhibit 332.2, we haven't yet reached that. The dates don't compare, but we've had, at considerable length, evidence of what happened in December '92 until January of '93, so that can be taken shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've finished with it, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If that's a convenient moment, we'll resume at a few minutes after half past 2.00. Doctor, we're going to adjourn now. If you would be back, please, for half past 2.00 to start. Could you remember, in this adjournment and any other adjournments, not to speak to anybody about your evidence, please? And that does include members of the Prosecution. Thank you. If you would be back then. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.01 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, we come to January 1993 and the war presidency. Very shortly, whose idea was it that such presidency should be created?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war presidency of the municipality of Vitez was founded on the basis of a decree of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We complied with it and established that body, which in wartime conditions was the supreme authority in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Republic had instructed you to set this up; was it a body that was to comprise people of all ethnicities, or just of one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was to consist of representatives of all peoples who lived in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there difficulties in finding somebody who was prepared to act as president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vitez, it was four persons who were nominated. They all refused. They did not dare. They tried to prevail upon me, and were at me for about -- more than a month, trying to talk me into accepting it. They believed that I was on good terms with everybody in Vitez and that therefore I would be successful and manage to prevent any conflict. Sometime on the 2nd of February, '93, I agreed to do that, as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What warnings, if any, had you had about the consequences of accepting this job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Croat from Vitez -- before the war, he was a high official in the republic and MUP, his name was Jugoslav Bilic -- and he came to my house and warned my wife and me that in Vitez, there was no room for Muslims any more. He offered to give us passports with Dario Kordic's signature, and we only had to write our names and the names of our children as Croat names, and he offered also to give us a ride to Split. I told him what I was being offered in Vitez, and he said, "Doctor, this is no joke; the situation is very serious. Think about it. I am at your disposal. Just give me two pictures of your children, and write down the names that you would like to have." My wife was frightened, but I thought there was an understanding reached on the 27th of January to set up a joint government to be called the municipal wartime government, municipality of Vitez, within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so it would be the wartime government of Vitez. It was in Grude, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, wartime government of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sorry, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatian Community, Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The original question was, what, if any, warnings did you have of what would happen to you if you took this job. Did you get any warnings of what would happen to you? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already said that I was warned by Bilic, Jugoslav Bilic, nicknamed Jugo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What would happen to you? Did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was in general terms, that there was no room for Muslims, that they would expel all Muslims, that the situation was serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's fine. The government having been set up, a parallel government, as I think you described it, did it have any dealings with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whom do you mean? I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You, having become president of the war presidency, did that presidency have dealings thereafter with the HVO? Did you meet them, the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, we already had reached agreement at the level of the BH army, signed by Sefer Halilovic and Milivoj Petkovic, as the commander in chief of the HVO, to set up three commissions in Vitez, mixed commissions, and a central one in Busovaca, and all incidents that would happen were to be investigated jointly. So one commission was the commission for incidents; another one was the commission for exchange of captured and exchange of our equipment and materiel; and the third commission was for the unimpeded return of military vehicles of the army of B and H to Vitez. In Busovaca, in Hotel Tisa, the joint commission sat. I think the army of B and H was represented by Dzemal Merdan; he was the chairman of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to stop you short: Did the commissions in Vitez meet? Just yes or no. Were they effective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long did they remain effective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the 15th of April, '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Between the summer of 1992 and the 15th -- I beg your pardon; start again. Between January and the 15th of April of 1993, were there further acts of violence committed against Muslims? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you can provide detail of and answer questions about those events if asked by either Defence counsel or by the Court? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already dealt with the destruction of the bank, which I think happened in January; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want now to move to the 15th of April and the next few days after the 15th of April of 1993, but just before I do, one question. Covering the whole period from the summer of '92 until April of '93, you've spoken of acts of violence by Croats against Muslims. Were there any acts of retaliation, to your knowledge, by Muslims on Croats? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were any of those in your presence? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were any of them with your approval?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I insisted that they all be taken under custody, detained, and punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that again we can deal with it shortly, first of all, you are in a position to give detail to the Defence counsel, if they want to know of it, of acts by Muslims, can you pick out a bad one, i.e., the worst example you can think of, of an act of retaliation or violence by Muslims committed on Croats in that period of time, and just tell us about that in a sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean after the murder of two soldiers, towards the end of November, on the road Kruscica/Vitez, members of the BH army captured six HVO members, and they were physically ill-treated. Not only -- one of them was ill-treated with a knife on the back. I intervened and saw that these men be released and that the soldiers of the BH army who had done that be detained by the military police and taken to the military prison in Zenica. As far as I know, those soldiers were arrested and taken to prison. I really don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's as much as I want of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course, Your Honour, in dealing with that, I'm not conceding relevance, but it seemed that a balanced picture was helpful, and it is available in more detail if it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 15th of April, then, of 1993: On that day, can you detail what was happening politically, or what did happen politically on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day, I was at my regular job as a physician, and I was called in to adjudicate at the meeting of the incidents commission. I was told that I had to arrange for the meeting of the war presidency. At the meeting, there was the incidents commission present, and I said that they concluded that the situation had deteriorated terribly in Vitez and that we had to hold a joint party meeting and a meeting of the representatives of the authorities to start the initiative on setting up joint command; that is, joint police and joint authority. They also suggested as to who should be invited from the regional level. I think they mentioned Asim Fazlic, who was the commander of the centre for security service in Zenica, and also the commander of the HVO civilian police for Central Bosnia, and also a representative of the Armija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you make arrangements with the HVO to attend such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We agreed and confirmed that a meeting would be held in the building of the municipal hall in Vitez on the 16th of April at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you then go home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the way home, on foot, I think, did you meet someone, some member of the HVO government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because my car had been stolen already, so I walked home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. His name was Zvonko Bekavac. He was a member of the HVO government in Vitez. I asked him to give me a lift home because my mother was ill -- because his mother was ill, so I went to his house to see his mother, to examine her and all that. After that, two other Croats came to Zvonko Bekavac's house and asked me to go and extend medical help for a woman, and they brought me an X-ray of her heart. I prescribed what to administer her and told them to take her to Travnik, to hospital, if her state did not improve. He also gave me a lift home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that's a Croat or Croats you were helping on that very night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was helping them. Yes, they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. That night, on the telephone, did you receive calls about the condition in Vitez generally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Many Muslims from Vitez called me, asking me what was going on, how to listen to television, and I answered -- I gave them all the same answer, that the next morning we would be having a meeting at 12.00 and there was no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next morning at 5.00, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next morning, around 5.30, and my wife and my parents-in-law was with me, my children and I were awakened by tremendous detonations, a series of detonations. Until that time, there were detonations here and there, but now there were tremendous detonation and a whole series of them. So we got up, and I dialled -- I called by telephone Sefkija Dzidic, the commander of the TO in Vitez, to ask him what it was all about, and he told me that Vitez had been attacked by the HVO, that fighting was going on around houses in Stari Vitez. I asked him what to do, and he told me, "Just stay at home and keep quiet." At that time, somebody rang at my door.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my neighbour, Marinko Katava from the second floor. So my wife and I opened the door. "Good morning, neighbour. So what is it about," I asked him, and he said, "I warned you that your children should not shout slogans, 'Armija, B and H' and not to write graffiti on the walls, and you did not obey. Now don't be surprised because HVO soldiers will come and you are no more," and he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had your children, to your knowledge, been chanting slogans, or had they been drawing graffiti?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know; nor did he warn me previously. I never talked about such things with Marinko Katava, and I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you stay in your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so. I mean they were small, my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you stay in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed in my apartment with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you receive further phone calls, informing you of things that had been happening in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was receiving all sorts of telephone calls. Some were provocative. Some were why don't I come out to help people. They were letting me know who had been killed. And finally my line was cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a matter of detail, "Yes" or "No". Was one of the people of whose death you were informed Nedim Zlotrg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you see them again, and if so, at what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My neighbour came again around 9.00 or 10.00 and asked me to go to the children's room to have a tête-à-tête conversation, and we entered. He brought me two boxes of cigarettes and asked me, "Doctor, tell me, what is it that you have done for all these people so that they saved your neck?" And I started telling them that I was a physician, but he was pressing on me to tell him who was it, because somebody was saving me, and that all this would be over by Monday. At that moment, another neighbour of mine came from the next-door, also a Croat, Dragan Safradin, of whom I was on very good terms, an engineer in Vitez, and he was crying. He also brought me a box of cigarettes and told me to keep quiet, to sit there, that I would have no more problems, that I had survived. I don't know. After that, they left, both of them. During that day, a third --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come to the third neighbour or third visitor, that first neighbour, Marinko Katava, did you get on well or not with that neighbour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His wife worked in the same company as I did. He was a pharmaceutical technician, so we cooperated, I mean, on medical issues. We were not close friends, but we were not enemies, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [indiscernible] before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. On one occasion, he came to my place with his wife and brought -- allegedly, the HVO government had given him the first aid kit, and they were taking it from the city pharmacy, and did I want to take part in this. I was telling him that this was city pharmacy and that the HVO could not make presents out of something which was city property. But otherwise, no, we did not have any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I'm having to cut you short, but it is the only way we can move the evidence forward swiftly in the way that is appropriate in this case, and I hope you don't think it's rude of me. But indeed I see that by doing that, I sometimes blank out the questions on the transcript. So what is indiscernible at line 7 is, "Had he shown any antagonism before," but I'm afraid that's going to happen as long as I have to cut through the answers of the witness from time to time. You stayed in your house. You were about to tell us about a third visitor, I think. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The third visitor was Stipo Krizanac, and one of -- [indiscernible] Safradin, who was in the next entrance to the house. Stipo came and asked me if we had any weapons in the house, and we said we didn't. He said that HVO soldiers would be searching flats and houses and would kill those in whose flats they did find weapons. I did not know -- I was not aware of any weapons in my house. When Stipo Krizanac left, my wife told me that Harum Suljevic, my neighbour from the floor above, had brought, meanwhile, four hand grenades and that they were on the balcony. My wife had packed them in a bag and took them to Stipo Krizanac's flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a search of your flat for weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you stay in your flat or in the building of your flat all day the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The following day, the 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the 18th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you receiving phone calls still?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first day, but also on the 17th and 18th, not so often. We were not allowed to go out. In front of the entrance to the building, there were armed men who were not allowing any kind of movement to members of my family and others. Anyway, I didn't go out. We were told that there were guards in front of the door, and through the windows I saw other entrances being guarded by armed men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From your phone calls or from any other callers, were you learning of what was happening in Vitez and, indeed, in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The wife of my colleague, Dzevad Balto called me up, and he was the director of the health centre in Vitez, and he said to me, "Why don't you go out?" Then after that, the woman looking through the window fell ill, and she got an acute psychosis. I don't think she ever recovered. Then some other people called me, without introducing themselves. They told me that a man called Salem Topcic was lying stabbed in the middle of the road, and he used to work in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm pausing there, and again in the most general terms, can you give any estimate of the number of deaths that were reported to you in -- local deaths that were reported to you in this period of time? You told us about the man Zlotrg, and you just told us about another. Were any other deaths reported to you about this period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received information that Arifa, I think her name was Tunovic, had been killed, and she had been a teacher in Vitez, in the elementary school there. Judovarupa Zlotrg, Mira Zlotrg, Salem Topcic. I later learned from Buzuka (phoen) that Saban Mahmutovic had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able to see or hear any shooting, either from light weapons or from heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I watched from my window as shells were falling on the village of Novaci. I saw houses in Stari Vitez burning and houses in Vitez owned by Muslims, the Kavazovic family. I think his name was Smajo. Koca, Ahmici, from that direction, I could see smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did your neighbour from the other floor, Marinko Katava, visit you again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said that he came to visit me between 9.00 and 10.00 on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no, on later days, moving beyond the 15th. Did he come on a subsequent day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Marinko Katava again on Sunday afternoon. He was going around and telling tenants to half open the windows because there would be an explosion and the panes could break. My father-in-law opened the windows, and in the afternoon, about 5.00, there was a very powerful explosion. Katava came around again, telling people not to be afraid, that it was an ammunition dump that had been hit at -- Djudin's garbage dump, because it was looked after by somebody called Djudin. I can't remember exactly his full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you subsequently discover what that explosion had been caused by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I later learned that where the offices of the war presidency of Vitez municipality had been, had been destroyed, that building had been destroyed. I think about eight people were killed on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And destroyed by what device?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later, I saw some photographs. At the time, I was living in the part of Vitez under full control of the HVO. Later, I saw remnants of a lorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And these offices that were destroyed, were they in Vitez or in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Earlier on, we didn't describe and divide Vitez into "Vitez" and "Stari Vitez", but it was in Stari Vitez that this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a clip of a video that I would like to show now. It's Z204.2. It was disclosed to the Defence, I think, in the summer of last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The position is this, Dr. Mujezinovic, isn't it? You subsequently saw the damage, and you can tell us if we've got it right, in this extract of the video, whether this video shows the damage caused by that truck bomb? So if that video could be played.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, but I'm not seeing anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we freeze there, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are the consequences --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can freeze it there, the image.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were the consequences of the lorry bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. It doesn't freeze frame very well. If we could just run it forward just a little further, and then that will be enough. Run it at normal speed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we see any particular building as we pass through that you can identify? This one or this one (indicating)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one to the right (indicating). This is Karahodzija Huzo's (phoen) house, and across the way there's a house that wasn't completely destroyed but which houses the offices of the war presidency. This is Huzo Karahodzija's (phoen) house in Vitez, and in this house did we have our offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was on the Sunday evening that that bomb happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the afternoon. In the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened next, so far as you were concerned? Did you stay in the flat, or did you go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Monday, the 19th, a soldier came to my apartment, an HVO soldier, a military policeman. I knew him; his name was Dragan Calic. He used to be in the TO. He was looking for me. My mother-in-law asked, "What do you want of him?" And I came out and said, "Dragan, what do you want?" And he said that I should take my doctor's bag and follow him, not to be afraid, that they had many wounded soldiers, that I had to go to work. He took me to the crafts centre, in the basement, which was the alternate position of the medical centre in Vitez. On the way, he asked me, "Do you know, Doctor, who saved your life?" I said I didn't know. And he told me that it was Darko Kraljevic who had saved my life, who had come by, by chance, when HVO soldiers were passing in groups, and he had ordered them that they mustn't kill me. When they had brought me to this reserve medical centre, the staff was surprised to see me alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there some nurses there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were doctors, nurses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had you by this stage learnt anything of the events in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until this point in time I knew nothing about Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the course of the day, two nurses from Ahmici told me what had happened in Ahmici. The name of one of them was Vidovic Santic. She didn't use to work in the medical centre before. And the other's name was Ljubas; that was her maiden name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember her name. They told me that the two of them, because they were Croat, had been moved, all of them, about 1.00 at night towards the Lasva Valley, and that in the morning, the HVO had attacked the village from all directions, that they had killed everything in their way, women, children, animals, and torched everything. When they told me about this, they were crying. They said that the situation in Ahmici was terrible, that there were many cows wandering around, many corpses lying there. That is when I learned about Ahmici. The other nurse's name is Ankica Pudza.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And by whom had those two nurses, according to them, been told to move at 1.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're now, then, in the medical centre, reserve medical centre. How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there roughly until the 15th or 19th of May, it was a Monday, when I was exchanged. Or maybe -- I think it was the 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to deal with some details in the course of that time, but before I do, are you saying that you didn't go back to your flat in the meantime? You stayed permanently in this complex? Or did you go back to your flat from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, occasionally one of the people with me, and there were three, I was told his name was Dragan Petrovic, known as Kinez, I was told that he was in charge of the organisation of work. When I had to go home, he would take me by ambulance to my entrance, it was about 200 to 300 metres away, and he would hand me over to the guards at the entrance. Also he would come and pick me up in the same way, and he would bring me back, when there was nothing to do, he would come in the daytime or at night, which means he would drive me to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps we'd better look at a map and just see if we can make a little more life of the geography. That is not going to take us very long. Z2186.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There should be a pointer on the desk, Dr. Mujezinovic, I don't know if there is, because the item will be put on the ELMO device -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure that a great deal turns on the geography, so I'm not going through the process, that is time-consuming, of marking the plan; that can always be done, if it turns out to be material, in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does this aerial view show part of Vitez? If you'd like it another way, differently oriented, say so, because it's sometimes difficult to follow maps other than in the way you like them. Move it round if you want.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a part of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you show us, please, any of the locations that you've been referring to, starting with your own address? You have to point on the ELMO, if you would be good enough. You have to point on that -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the other microphone be switched on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And they would drive me along here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that was the medical centre there, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The location of the offices that were blown up by the truck bomb, are they shown or not shown on this plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they're not. This is a neighbourhood that we called "Kolonija," and in this area here is that other part of Vitez (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Off the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Off the map; very well. So that was the comparatively short journey that you had to be driven from the flat to the hospital and back again, under guard at all times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was just driven by Dragan Petrovic. There was no guard. But he would hand me over to the guards at the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, shortly after being taken to this location, did you have a meeting with the defendant Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same day, in the evening, about 8.00, to the medical centre where I worked at the time, two military policemen came. The name of one of them was Anto Kovac, known as Zabac, and the other was Ratko Nuk. They ordered me to follow them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where did you land up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The medical staff asked me, "Where are you going, Doctor?" And they just told me to go. They took me to the cultural centre in Vitez, or the Workers' University, to the command. I didn't know until then that that was where Cerkez's command was, that is, in the cultural centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that shown on this plan, this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the cultural centre in Vitez (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. When you got there, what did you find, and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These soldiers, or rather military policemen, took me into the office where, sitting at a long table, was Mario Cerkez together with Zeljo Sajevic, Zvonko Cilic, Borislav Jozic, Zeljo Vrebac, Stipe Zigonja. I knew all of them very well. Most of them used to work in the TO staff, as professionals, whereas Zvonko Cilic worked as a social worker and Borislav worked in the security of the factories in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were these all Croats, or was there a mixture of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was said to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mario Cerkez asked me whether I was aware of the position I was in. I said yes. He asked me whether I knew about Ahmici. I said yes. Then he said to me, in that case, I had to do as he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did you interpret the combination of questions about Ahmici and being obliged to do what you were told?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood it as a threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think it's going a little bit beyond. (Interpretation) It seems to me that the question is not appropriate. Perhaps the question could be rephrased, because this is in a sense a leading question. An opinion is required of the witness rather than facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, in fact, it's not a leading question. It was not asked in leading form. And the witness can answer as to how he interpreted what was said. That is matter of fact, as to how he interpreted it. Whether it is or is not a threat, of course, is something for us. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the next thing that Cerkez said to you or told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said to me, "Doctor, you know where Dubravica and Zabrdze are?" The BH army had broken through the front lines at Dubravica and Zabrdze. He said to me that I must call up the command of the 3rd Corps, that there were 2.223 prisoners of war, and if they continued their advance on Vitez, that he would order the killing of those prisoners. I knew Dugalic Ramiz in the 3rd Corps, who is from Vitez, and who used to work in the TO staff in our town at one time. I sat at a table opposite them. Zvonko Cilic was there, too, next to me. I called up Ramiz Dugalic in the 3rd Corps, and I told him what Mario Cerkez asked me to say: That there were 2.223 prisoners, and if the BH army continued its advance on Vitez, that he would order the execution of the prisoners. He also told me that I had to call up the Bosnian politicians, Izetbegovic, Ganic. I asked Ramiz Dugalic to give me their telephone numbers. Ramiz Dugalic wanted to know what telephone number I was calling from. He called me back half an hour later and told me that I should accept all the terms set by Cerkez, that he would order a halting of the attack on Vitez. After that, Mario Cerkez said that I had to address the Muslims of Stari Vitez on television and ask them to surrender their weapons. I sort of hesitated, and then he gave me Zvonko Cilic to assist me as to the way in which I should speak, but first he asked me to set up a commission for negotiations with the HVO. I said to Mario Cerkez --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you for one short question before we move on to what happened next: When Cerkez told you about the HVO lines having been broken through, did you know that to be true, or did you discover that that was true, and one way or another, was what he said about the village of Dubravica shown subsequently to be true, or not? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment I did not know, but later I learned that it was true, when I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, very well, then. You'd been instructed to set up a commission to negotiate. Did that lead to your going to the basement of those premises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I said to Mario Cerkez, I asked him who should be at those negotiations, and he just waved his and said, "Doctor, in the basement there are 300 men; you can choose who you like. I don't care." I went to the basement with Zvonko Cilic and the soldiers -- or rather the military policemen -- and in the basement I found a host of people in the basement, where the coal was for heating the building. There were men between 18 and perhaps 70 years of age, from all these neighbourhoods, the Muslims from Kolonija, professors, teachers, engineers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What were the conditions in which they were kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know what a place looks like where you shovel coal into a furnace for central heating?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many people there? Could they stand up, sit down, lie down? Describe the position -- in a few sentences, but so that we can have a picture of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mario Cerkez himself told me that there were about 300 of them. These were cellars, really, with small windows for shovelling in coal. The ventilation was very poor. There were too many people. It was too crowded. There wasn't enough room for people to stand comfortably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who did you select, quickly -- not quickly, fairly swiftly, so far as names are concerned -- and what criteria did you apply to select people for this so-called commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I mostly took -- picked out intellectuals from Vitez. Sivro, who was an electrical engineer, he was director of research and development at Vitezit; Mulah Halilovic, he was the director of the secondary school in Vitez; Kadir Dzidic, who was a professor in Vitez; Fuad Kadir, who was the president of the executive board in Vitez, and a young man about whom I knew he had heart valves built in. I'm not sure of his name; I think it's Nuzja (phoen) Bilic. They all set off except for Kaknjo, who was too afraid. We went to the office of Muazam Gerim, and he was there, too. Formerly he was the SPS director in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there any, and if so what sort of number of people in the basement, dressed in military uniform, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they all wore civilian clothes. They were all civilians, and in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So back to the office: What happened in the office with your commission as now formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the office, where Zvonko Cilic and Boris Jozo were there in the office, and they insisted that Fuad Kaknjo come too. So we went back to fetch him, and he also came to the office. In this office, Zvonimir Cilic and Borislav Jozic said to those present what they were expected to do: To call their acquaintances by telephone and to tell them that they were in a basement, that they were about 300 of them, that the BH army should stop attacking, that they would all be killed, and the like. And Zvonko Cilic and I agreed and around 1.00 after midnight I was taken to the upper floor to address the public in Vitez. So we drew up a text, and the local television then broadcast it every now and then for about a couple of days, with my statement. When I finished that, I returned to the office around 2.00, Cilic and Jozic said they had to go, and they said that if we wanted to stay in that office, we could, and if not, we could go back to the cellar. They promised that we would come to talk to -- that Pero Skopljak and Ivan Santic would come around 6.00 in the morning to talk to us. We stayed in this office and only Fuad Kaknjo went down to the cellar. Around 5.00 in the morning, Pero Skopljak turned up, and Ivan Santic, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You didn't go down to the cellar again? Or did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only Fuad Kaknjo went down to the cellar. We stayed in that office, at the desk, and every half hour an HVO guard would enter to see what we were doing. And as a matter of fact, we were just sitting, I mean, there was nowhere to lie down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Cerkez had mentioned 2.223 prisoners of different gender and age. You'd seen about -- or you'd seen what you were told was 300 men. Were you informed of where any other prisoners were being kept, and if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cerkez said that he had 2.223 prisoners. At that time, I did not know even about those in the cellar. I didn't know where the others were being kept until I heard it from Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did he tell you about where the others were kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not tell me where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did anybody else tell you where the others were being kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on, I learnt, when I came out, after that night, later, I heard and I saw prisoners in the SDK office, that was the public auditing service in Vitez, and I asked Bruno Buzuk to set free a veterinarian who had had four bypasses on his heart. He was in the cellar of the veterinarian station, or rather in his surgery, where he examined animals. Later they brought Dr. Patkovic, Dr. Muris Trako. Dr. Muris Trako told me that he had been detained in the elementary school in Dubravica, and he told me there were women, children, and adult men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you look, please, at the next exhibit, 752.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I take it we're on target?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. I had actually forgotten what time we sit to this afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just after 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I should hope so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document -- I'm sorry about the quality of the original -- is described as a joint statement dated the 20th of April of 1993, and it has at its foot signatures over the typed names of yourself and Ivan Santic. It is in five paragraphs, of which the first is a demand that the military commands of HVO and BH army establish a cease-fire. The second is that the civilian representatives unanimously declare that there should be -- no conflict would have arisen without the influence of global politics. The third, in capital letters, reads that: "SINCE MANY PEOPLE HAVE ALREADY BEEN KILLED, WOUNDED AND CAPTURED, WE REQUEST THAT THE MILITARY COMMANDERS ACT IN ACCORDANCE WITH INTERNATIONAL HUMANITARIAN STANDARDS AS SOON AS POSSIBLE." The fourth, that, "Both sides agree that in Vitez and Province 10, the Vance-Owen Plan should be implemented even before signed by the Serbian side. Also, the army shall retain their structure in conformity with the ethnic composition ..." And five, "The highest-level civilian government bodies shall immediately establish a political dialogue which will continue until there is a permanent peace." That document has a signature; is it yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is the document in any sense truly your document, in that you drafted it or agreed to it with free will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was signed in the morning of the 20th, when Pero Skopljak and Ivan Santic came that morning. Then Santic suggested that we write this, and suggested -- I don't know whether he brought the text of the agreement with him, as I already had the consent to sign. Whatever the HVO would request us to sign in Vitez, I would have of course signed it, except that I did not agree with Item 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So did you not agree with the proposition that civilian representatives unanimously declare that no conflict would have arisen without global politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian representatives of the Croatian and Muslim peoples declare that the conflict would not have arisen again. Because in your translation, if it were not for the influence of global politics and military operations from the outside of the municipality. I still think -- and I thought that we had done everything, absolutely everything, to avoid a conflict and humiliation and insults and plunder and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. I can move on, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- tremendous human effort --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can move on to the remaining period of time that you spent in Vitez. You've already dealt with it in summary. Between the 20th of April and the time when you left Vitez in May, did you carry on treating the sick, so far as you were able, sick and injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They perceived me as their chief, so I selected the wounded -- that is, I decided which wounded should go to Split, which to Travnik, to Zenica, and who could stay in our hospital and be treated there. Meanwhile nobody asked for me, nobody called me. My family were not harassed. On the door of my apartment there was a poster, which said that I was an HVO physician, with a stamp. And really, I worked, and I had no problems. Even some Croats from Vitez, because I knew a number of them, even gave me some money and would tell me, "well, now, you need this, so this is for you." Twice a week, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [No microphone] ... or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only HVO's wounded soldiers came, and they were Muslim civilians, but not members of the BH army. They were simply not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So when people were giving you money, was it because it because you'd treated them as a doctor, or were they giving you money for other reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not because I treated them, but they were saying, "you will need this." They simply gave it to me. I remember one of them, Niko Marac (phoen), suffering from cirrhosis of the liver, and I treated him, and he simply said, "Well, listen, Doctor, do you need any money?" And I told him no, I did not need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move now to the 19th of May of 1993. Did you go to work in accordance with your then pattern on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went to work on the 19th, or perhaps 18th, or was it 19th? It was Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was one other question I should have asked: I'll deal with it now. Between the 15th of April and this day, the 18th or 19th of May, had you been able to exercise any political authority, or to take part in any political functions and matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the presidency of which you were the president still in existence, technically? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it able to operate? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And back to this day, the 18th or 19th: You went to work. Who drove you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was always driven by Petrovic, Dragan Petrovic, from my flat to work. Twice a week I went to Busovaca to work, and then a driver from Busovaca would come. At first, I and Dr. Muris Trako went -- he was a surgeon. And later on, he left, and I went all by myself twice a week, Tuesdays and Thursdays, first to examine the wounded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us keep to the point, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that day, were you driven away from work in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the 18th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the 18th or the 19th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 18th of May, I received a call from Dr. Bruno Buzuk. He asked me if I would like to see my mother. My mother lived not far from Vitez, and it was under the control of the BH army. Would I like to see my mother? I thought he was pulling my leg, but at 12.00, Dr. Bruno came, called the driver of the medical unit, Dragan Bugojnoic, and told me to sit in the back. I sat there, and he took me to the checkpoint of the BH army at Dubravica. On the other side was an ambulance car of the 3rd Corps, with a unit of the 3rd Corps and Dr. Alija Smajlovic, and they took out a woman from the Zenica ambulance car, and I moved into the -- and they put her into the car in which I had driven up, and I moved into the ambulance car that had come from Zenica. Dr. Alija Smajlovic said that that was the wife of a Croat general, that they had heard that I was to be killed, that there was Kordic's order, Dario Kordic's order, that I should come to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On what grounds are you objecting?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This is absolute hearsay, and I think that it's unduly prejudicial under the test of Rule 89 for reasons that we stated when we went over the same kind of testimony with Witness A on April 13th. Apparently the declarant is not listed as a witness. We don't even know whether the declarant supposedly saw this order, and there's simply no way to test the veracity of it. I think that the prejudicial impact of this testimony grossly outweighs any limited probative value it would have, if it has any, which I don't think that it has. So for those reasons, we object to that testimony, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I know Your Honour is probably about to make a ruling. You haven't heard from me yet, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid we haven't heard from you. Normally, no discourtesy is intended, but we have considered the matter fully and we're going to exclude it. It's what somebody has said that somebody else has said that he's heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I must interrupt the Court, because the Court hasn't heard me. I'm afraid that's not, with great respect, fair, because there is further supporting evidence in respect of this. When you come to this type of evidence, it's important to look at the position in the round. Now here you have a man who is working according to a routine imposed on him, substantially under control and effective imprisonment for part of the day. Those who plainly -- and we only heard of one so far, but those who had his interests at heart changed his routine and moved him from a place where it may be judged, on all the evidence as well as this category of evidence, that he was at risk, and moved him to a position of safety. So that, in itself, goes to show, as a matter of evidence, that there was a risk. We now have to trace where that risk comes from. If you had permitted the evidence in, and I'm going to ask you to reconsider the position and to hear, before you hear the detail of it, the outline of the other material that goes to support, when you hear all the evidence from two different sources that goes to point, to the same conclusion, then you may conclude, and I would invite you to say that you must conclude, that each can support the other, the two separate bits of evidence, and in any event, in all the circumstances, it's more likely to be of some value than of no value, it's more likely to be right than wrong. The people who would be protecting this man from the risks that the independent evidence of his being moved shows existed, are the sort of people who it's always going to be difficult for us to have first-hand because of their proximity themselves to the defendants, and it may be because of their doing things that were contrary to their own code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But just pause a moment and think what you're submitting. Because the case is difficult to prove, are you saying, "We should have the thinnest sort of evidence in?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that appears to be the effect of the submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that at all. But I am inviting the Court, in a place where hearsay of any generation is not automatically excluded, to have in mind, amongst other things, the difficulties of getting first-hand evidence. That's just something to have in mind. But more important, to look at the surrounding circumstances, which I've touched on, and the other evidence which would have been or would be evidence in support. I'll explain in general, although I don't want to rehearse the witness, where it comes from. It comes from a meeting he had the night before and with someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, why don't you deal with that evidence, if you say you've got it, and we'll consider that. But at the moment, this evidence is not to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And may I make this point as well, just in general before I move on? Where we're dealing with evidence coming from other sources, as it's been described, secondhand, it may be important for the Court to have some regard to the sort of person from whom the witness in court hears that which comes to him. As I think Your Honour said on an earlier occasion, it's always a question of reliability that's at root, and therefore if the evidence comes from somebody who is likely to be reliable in all the circumstances, or likely to be unreliable, that will affect your judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, the night before this exchange, on your way from where you were doing your work, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken on Friday, that is, two days earlier. I was asked by a Croat to examine his mother. That Croat's mother had been to see me and was examined by me a couple of days earlier. That Croat took me to his uncle's house, where his mother was, and she was making some dough. So I said, "Good afternoon, good afternoon. How are you?" And she said, "Fine." That person --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're going to deal with the evidence in small bits for the convenience of everyone. First of all, are you happy to name in this Tribunal here now, in the present circumstances, the Croat who took you to his mother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, I told you already, during closed session, I can't name. But I already was in the courtroom and I already testified about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the name of this person, if you can name him --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is Vujica Trpimir. He taught biology in Vitez. He was a Croat by ethnicity. He took me into the room and said he had taken to UNPROFOR bases Dr. Enesa Mulalic the day before. And Dragan Petrovic was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The mother who you were taken to see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we can cut to the central matter here. I believe that Mr. Nice is trying to elicit from the witness precisely the same kind of hearsay testimony, from someone who is not on the witness list, by the way, Mr. Vujica, apparently, to the effect that he heard from someone that there was the same kind of order about which he's previously testified, and that evidence has been excluded. This evidence should be excluded for precisely the same reasons. In the Rule 89 balance, Your Honour, and I don't think we've made too many of these objections, but in the Rule 89 balance, you have to balance the prejudicial effect, which is substantial, against the probative value, which is virtually zero. I think that for the same reasons, this testimony should be omitted. It's rank double or triple hearsay and it's very prejudicial, and we object to it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's hear a bit more of the evidence first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So now the mother you had been taken to look at or to treat because she was unwell or apparently unwell, in fact, in what condition was she when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that man took me into the room, took out a bottle of brandy, and poured for the two of us, and said, "Doctor, Dragan Petrovic in Skopljak has been put in charge of controlling what you are doing."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you again. It's difficult, I know, to understand the reasons for these small questions with requests for short answers, but I hope, Doctor, you'll accept that there is a reason for it. When you saw the woman, what condition was she; fit or unfit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was okay. I saw her in the house of her brother. She was making a pie, as I was saying, the dough for a pie.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that you had been taken to see somebody who was apparently unfit, but she now appeared to be well. The man who talked to you, don't tell Their Honours yet what the man said. Tell us a bit more about the man. What sort of man was he? What did he do for a living? You've mentioned it, but repeat it. Just tell us what sort of chap he was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a teacher of biology in Vitez. He was teaching in grammar school. I didn't know him from before. I knew the family, I knew his father, but until that time, I had not known him personally. He was a young man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know anything to his detriment, did you know anything to his credit, up until this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, we have to object again. The witness, in answer to a question, said that he didn't know the man. After that came another question in the same direction. I think the Prosecution is repeating the same questions that have already been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the evidence was he knew his father, "but I had not known him personally." Yes, yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know anything to his detriment, did you know anything to his credit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, move on from that. Very well, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Mujezinovic, don't say anything that's material to your particular position on this day, because that's what the Court is concerned about. But did this man who poured you a brandy, did he tell you anything about the general scope of his function? First of all, just "Yes" or "No". Do you understand my question? I only want you to tell the Court what he told you was his function at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then tell us, please, what he told you was his function.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did he tell you was his function?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His function was to secure the place we were working. Not just his function; he also mentioned the names of two other men involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he say anything about his function in relation simply to your movements; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He said that it was his duty to follow what I was doing, whom I talked to, how I was working, and that he had to report to the HVO about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he tell you how long he had been doing that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the very beginning, when the conflict started, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just "Yes" or "No". You had a further conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I started to work --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Stop there. I just wanted to stop it at that. Now, I've laid the groundwork. The Court, not having read the material, won't know precisely what's forthcoming. But from the necessary formulation of the argument, it will know, in general terms, what will be forthcoming. Since the Court has to wear hats both as the decider of law and the decider of fact, it may prefer to know, even now, precisely what would be forthcoming. But that's a matter for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is entirely without prejudice to admissibility. We shall hear the evidence. I'm afraid I'm not going to take any more argument at this stage. We wish to hear the evidence, and then we'll rule on it. If we decide it's inadmissible, then we shall exclude it entirely. At least I want to know the basis on which it's being put forward. Yes. Mr. Kovacic, we've really had a great deal of interruption. What do you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, I do not object to this. The ground has been laid. But I would suggest, for us to be on the safe side when judging hearsay, to ask the witness, before this question, another question, and that is whether this gentleman, the one he's talking about, is he alive or dead today?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm happy enough to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What's the answer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he's alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, can you now please tell the Court what else the man said to you at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said to me that they had received orders from Dario Kordic that when I come to Busovaca the next time, that is, on Tuesday, because I had been the previous Thursday, there was an order for me to be killed. He said to me, "My father asked me to save you and to take you to the UNPROFOR base in Stara Bila." As I had my children, my wife, my in-laws in Vitez --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. He told you that this is what he had learned. Did he explain how he had learned that, what his source of information was for where he learned of the order that you've described or that he described to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that they had received the order, that is, the HVO security that was providing the security for us who were working, and that there was a written order from Kordic that when I come to Busovaca the next time, I should be executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that's enough for now. Just a moment, Doctor. We will decide upon the admissibility of that. I take it that a written order does not --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The written order does not exist. I've made my argument about the two features having the potential to support each other and, indeed, this one arguably being much stronger than the one that in the event came up first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, could we know from the witness something that would clarify things? He said, "When I was going to Busovaca on the following Tuesday." What date would that be? What date would that Tuesday be?" "I had gone on a Thursday, and when I was going again on Tuesday." What date was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, can you help us with the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went every week on Tuesdays and Thursdays. This went on for a month, you see, --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We want the date, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- or maybe 20 days. I had been there on a Thursday. I think it was the 15th. I was told this on the 16th. And on the next Tuesday, I was due to go again to Busovaca to work there. I think it must have been the 19th of May, 1992. But I'm just mentioning that I went every week to work in Busovaca on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope that helps. If it was the 15th, by an addition of those numbers, it would actually be not the 19th but the 20th. I hope that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, just something I wasn't clear about. I believe the witness said that -- it has gone off the printout here -- that the HVO security had received the order. That was the effect of it. I wanted to find out whether the person of whom he's speaking was a part of that security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have the question, Doctor. Was this man speaking to you a part of that security --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was he saying to you, if anything, about whether he had or had not seen the order himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that all of them had seen it, that they had received such a signed order, and that his father, Slavko Vujica, had asked him to save my life, to get me out and to take me to the UNPROFOR base.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall exclude this evidence. We doubt its reliability. It is highly prejudicial. The question is, "What sort of weight, at the end of the case, could you put on this piece of evidence," and the answer is, "Very little." In those circumstances, it will be excluded. Of course, we are not establishing any sort of general principle. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have two more short topics. Do you want me to deal with them now or tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we're minded to adjourn, but if you could make them as short as possible overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the Defence will be ready first thing in the morning, I hope. Mr. Stein, are you undertaking the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, we would like and we've agreed amongst ourselves to have Mr. Kovacic begin and then Mr. Sayers, if that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kovacic, you'll be ready first thing tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I shall be ready, of course, in the morning, Mr. President. You may be interested in the duration of the cross-examination, but I believe it will be for the whole day, for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if we can get all the cross-examination in tomorrow, it would undoubtedly be a good thing, and we're going to do that. Doctor, could you be back, please, at 9.45 tomorrow morning and we'll go on with your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.16 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 11th day of May, 1999, at 9.45 a.m.
